quote: The fairest action of our human life / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
source: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, Act 4, the chorus that closes the act, lines 1 to 4 (1613) (Chorus)
speaker: Chorus
note: Corrected: line 2 ends in a colon, not a semicolon, in the 1613 quarto and in modern editions alike. The spelling here is modernised: the quarto prints humane, iniurie, aduersaries. The speaker is the chorus, a company of Jews who judge by their own lights, so the source names them.

evidence.where: Malone Society Reprint of the 1613 quarto (ed. A. C. Dunstan with W. W. Greg, 1914), full text read this run, plus a modernised annotated classroom text of Act 4 read as a PDF this run
evidence.edition: The Tragedy of Mariam, 1613 quarto, Malone Society Reprints 1914; wording modernised as standard editions print it
evidence.locator: the Chorus at the close of Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Malone reprint, beside line 1905; numbered about 628 to 631 in act line numbering)

reason: The quatrain is genuinely Cary’s and opens the chorus that closes Act 4, as the proposal said. Two independent texts agree that line 2 closes with a colon: the quarto reads Is scorning to reuenge an iniurie: and the modernised text reads Is scorning to revenge an injury:. The locator was also loose, since the quarto is in old spelling and the proposed wording is not, so the citation now says 1613 without claiming the quarto’s own letters.
